[h2]Short Game Description[/h2]
In Edna & Harvey: The Breakout, we play as Edna with its talking toy rabbit named Harvey, where we find ourselves at a mental hospital with amnesia, where we will start our adventure figuring out why we are locked there until we unravel the entire truth. This premise, combined with the point-and-click game, managed to create a very interesting adventure with original puzzles.
[list]
[*][h3]Positives[/h3]
Discussing the positives, first of all, the adventure that it brings managed a very unique and intriguing plot that featured charismatic characters; it also brought some humour, making the experience quite enjoyable. Secondly, as a point-and-click game, it does it very well with their original challenging puzzles, which will require you to think outside the box and be creative overall, as most of the puzzles you need to solve in order to advance are convoluted. Thirdly, the general setting and artistic style fit well and manage to better settle the theme along with the soundtrack. Additionally, the game offers you the opportunity to play with the classic artistic style however you want.
[*][h3]Negatives[/h3]
On the negative side, the main problem I had, which was not that huge, is that the ending could be a bit more detailed, as it feels quite rushed.
[/list][h2][u]Conclusion[/u][/h2]
In short, it is a great point-and-click game with an enjoyable plot and charismatic characters with an intriguing premise, where you will be unravelling the story throughout many challenging puzzles. The game is a 7.75/10.

Edna & Harvey is a classic point-and-click game with great storytelling, a charming art style, and a fun atmosphere. But it has one big problem: there’s no hint system.

I often struggle with Poki games because of how many riddles involve item combinations that don’t make sense right away. The pacing can also feel slow since you have to talk to every character to figure out what to do next.

While I love the art style and the unique storytelling, this game can feel frustrating. I struggled with Edna & Harvey: New Eyes, and even though I’ve played this one before and watched Let’s Plays of it, some parts are just too hard or confusing.

I still recommend the game because it’s creative and fun, but I can’t finish it without using a guide. For me, walking around endlessly, rereading dialogue, and constantly looking things up takes away the fun.

If you enjoy tough puzzles and don’t mind figuring things out on your own, you’ll probably love this game. But if you’re like me, it might test your patience more than your problem-solving skills.

Despite this, it remains my favorite point-and-click adventure and one of the funniest games I've ever played. For a trip down memory lane filled with insider jokes, it's worth having a walkthrough handy—after all, who could forget "Droggelbecher"!

The art style is super charming, like flipping through a beautifully weird cartoon, and the characters are just as memorable. It really captures that nostalgic point-and-click vibe while giving it a fresh polish. The only hiccup is the slightly clunky controls, which can be a bit of a puzzle themselves, but once you get the hang of it, it’s a joy to explore. Honestly, it’s an adorable little gem that stuck with me.

A fun and quirky old school point-and-click adventure game. It has clever and occasionally very tricky puzzles, and a host of wildly eccentric characters to interact with. There are a huge amount of unique responses for using every item on everything, and I had a very enjoyable time leisurely meandering around and trying various things while I was trying to solve the puzzles. The way the plot slowly unfolds also makes for a thrilling mystery that will have you piecing things together as you go, until it all comes together at the end. Though the dialogue is often lighthearted and comedic, as a game set in asylum, it still definitely contains some dark undertones here and there, and it doesn't pull its punches where it matters.

If there was one complaint I had, it was that there are a few minor visual bugs or disjointed animations in certain places that make it seem like you've solved a puzzle and it "didn't take", when you've actually only half-solved it and there are still steps remaining. The [spoiler]locking Babbit in the tower room[/spoiler] puzzle in particular made me think the game was bugged, when in truth, I actually just had one more thing I had to do to complete the puzzle.

All in all, if you're a fan of old school point-and-click games, and you don't mind a fiendish puzzle and a bit of visual jank now and then, you'll definitely enjoy this game. The writing is excellent and it's a ride from start to finish.

The artwork and atmosphere are charming and fit the tone of the game perfectly, though the pacing of the gameplay can feel uneven at times.

🌑 Conclusion
Edna & Harvey: The Breakout - Anniversary Edition is a fun and quirky adventure game with a lot of potential. The humor and puzzles are engaging, but the repetitive nature of some gameplay elements holds it back from being a truly standout experience. For fans of point-and-click adventures, it's still worth checking out, but be prepared for a few slower moments.

A tough one to review.

One of the best things was the huge amount of detail on every item interaction you can think of. I found myself combining items at random to see the jokes, and many of them were quite funny. These developers are very smart!

One of the worst things was the huge amount of detail on every item interaction you can think of. Because of that, it was nearly impossible to figure out what items were important or not, if anything I tried was close to a solution or was just a joke. This would be forgivable if the puzzles were easy to figure out... but some of the puzzles were "monkey-wrench" impenetrable to me (I might be getting old and impatient). Day of the Tentacle feels like a casual HOG next to this...

(Game developers know NOT to put detail in some places. In an action game, if a certain part of the level/town/scenery isn't detailed, if the textures there are boring, if the lighting is grey and flat, well, you feel no urge to go there, and the game flows better. For adventure games, it is the difference between "it's a door" or "this is the door to the pool room. The lock is shaped like a rabbit, and I can see a purple glow coming from under it.".)

Also: the game has a huge tonal variation. It is often funny, with dark undertones; and then it is dark, with (or without) funny undertones. This makes it very unique and interesting... but also causes "mood whiplash".

In summary, memorable story and characters and good sense of humor, but the puzzles were way too hard for me. An interesting game for sure, but for overall enjoyment, it is a "neutral" recommendation.

[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The game allows you to play the game with both original and remake visuals. I only saw the original visuals a bit when I tweaked the setting, but the visuals seem to be improved from the traditional art look to a digital, cartoonish-looking one. There is one animation that doesn't seem to be remade into a better version, but the transition isn't that obvious in the first place. Characters and backgrounds blend nicely with their same style, making it easy to focus on the story.

[h3]Story[/h3]
As a game that is placed in an asylum, it's obvious which kind of people that you'll interact with. The guards might look sane at first glance, although they still have traits that make them unique on their own. You might want to pay extra attention when talking to the other patients too. Their problems and sanity help to give color to the dialogues.

All dialogues are voice dubbed. Some character might exaggerate their voice, but it wasn't happening that often. The dialogues themselves are funny, yet unexpected at the same time. It was nice to see how the story unfolds, especially after knowing well of the characters' traits.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2639730493

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
Despite being a point-and-click game, the way to solve problems are a bit different from the other games in the same genre. You don't always have to use an object to another object to figure out a solution. You need to think about the solution in a broader term, figuring out other characters' characteristics and items that you possess. However, since the solution isn't obvious, it's easy to get stuck. It's not rare when I found that I couldn't find anything more to do after exploring all available locations since I didn't know that I could do something from the items that I have gathered.

Traveling around areas takes time, whether it's due to the animations or the events that unfold whenever you do something. Trying out some solutions might require you to go back and forth several times, wasting a lot of time in the process. It wasn't fun to get "punished" like this whenever you are trying to figure out what you need to do.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2639733764

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in 7h after experiencing both endings. There is no difference in the endings apart from the dialogue at the end, so you can always save the game before the story branches and load your save to experience both endings. I admit that I got stuck a lot when I was trying to figure out the solutions though. You need to think out of the box to solve them, and sometimes, things are not as obvious as you see. However, it was satisfying whenever you execute a plan flawlessly and figure out how to solve the problem yourself.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Edna & Harvey: The Breakout - Anniversary Edition[/b] does a good job both on its point-and-click and story elements. The point and click sections are unique with the out-of-the-box thinking while the story is interesting enough to entertain you. As someone who tends to get stuck with the point and click section, I enjoyed the story a lot. The mental patients give another charm to the story, and it was entertaining enough to see how characters are interacting with each other. I could easily recommend this if you like to play similar games, although you might want to be wary with the difficult point and click sections.

I got this game on sale and paid £3.49. Unlike some, I never played this when it first came out and have no nostalgia for it, although I accidentally played the sequel first so I had some idea about what was going on. As an anniversary edition it's exactly the same as the original, but with better graphics (although you can change it back to those original graphics in the settings) and without the bugs (if you have windows 10 this version is a must). Although I prefer the sequel, I still found this game enjoyable and fun to play. It's typical of it's genre, and recognizably a Daedalic game, in that there are some hard puzzles and a bit of back and forth is needed to collect the right items and continue. There are no English walkthroughs on the official steam page, but there are plenty online, and one on the original games steam page. There is a nice variety of environments and some fun characters to meet, although most you don't meet for very long. I personally found the story only ok, with some parts coming a bit too dramatically for my taste, whilst others were a bit slow and un-engaging The ending in particular wasn't as satisfying as I hoped, with what felt like a couple of loose threads such as [spoiler] who the key master really was [/spoiler] being left without being tied up. The achievements are fun, if a little grindy, and many of the optional achievements allow you find some cool dialogue options you may have missed. Personally it's not worth it's high price, and I only recommend it on sale for at least 50% off.

"Edna & Harvey: The Breakout" is a quirky, point-and-click adventure that’s often praised for its dark humor, offbeat storyline, and unique art style, making it a hit among fans of indie games and narrative-driven puzzles; players might describe it as a "mind-bending trip" or say it’s "packed with weird, hilarious, and creepy moments" that keep you hooked, with some calling it a "quirky gem" that’s perfect for those who love a good mental puzzle and a story with a dark, twisted vibe.

This was recommended by a friend during a sale but being a genre I don't play often I thought why not and so began my play through of Edna & Harvey: The Breakout. Being the anniversary edition the visuals have been given a touch up compared to the original while the audio still seems to be the same. You play as Edna with her stuffed rabbit Harvey and your goal is to break out of the asylum and to find answers about your past and why you've been locked up for many years.

Most of the time is spent exploring, gathering, crafting and talking to the facilities many weird and wonderful residents learning their stories or picking up useful bits of info or items. Some of these are straightforward and easy to do while others require trial and error especially if your not into these styles of games and accidentally overlook a detail or two that progresses the game further. Once you get used to how things are done it does get easier but also helps when your friend gives hints and tips after they finish having a chuckle   from watching you wander around with little clue as to whats going on.

So despite stumbling and fumbling around A LOT until I got into the games rhythm I still enjoyed myself so next time when it's on sale I'd recommend giving it a go as the story is enjoyable. Also thanks to my friend for pointing this one out :)

Original Edna & Harvey: The Breakout still plays fine, and this is a great remaster of an already classic point&click adventure. I would even call this version a remake since all backgrounds and characters were redrawn in higher resolution, with more details, and the game now supports 16:9 aspect instead of 5:4. You can also switch to the old version at any time, so it's basically a 2 in 1 product.

The only downside nowadays is probably the way the game is structured: practically the whole story unfolds in one big location featuring a lot of interactible objects, while Edna also gets to keep all the items she finds during this part. And since some of the puzzles are rather obscure, it might be pretty much impossible to finish the game without a walkthrough, because trial and error with so many items and objects is simply impossible. Even if you grew up playing Sierra and Lucas Arts adventures, I can assure you some of the puzzles will make your head explode.

There's an upside, however: Edna has unique comments for practically every combination of inventory items and game objects, and some of her remarks are hilarious. So even if you are trying to mix the unmixable, you will get a specifically written line. Moreover, some inventory items are asbolutely useless for walkthrough and are in the game just so you get to hear more of these quirky monologues (and earn some achievements as well).

Overall, a solid remake of a great point&click game. Definitely play it if you are a fan of the genre.

I don't enjoy giving negative reviews, especially to point-and-click adventure games, a genre that is very close to my heart. I've heard a lot of praise for Edna & Harvey over the years, so I went in with certain expectations that sadly weren't met.

There's a lot of good here: the world and its characters are charming, it is pretty upbeat most of the time, and it sports a ridiculous amount of interactions and voiced lines. You can seemingly combine anything with anything and get a unique line from the characters; I've never experienced anything like that. It definitely shows that the game was made with love for the genre and wanted to innovate on this often-overlooked aspect of its gameplay.

I dislike two things in adventure games, and Edna & Harvey sadly does both of them. Firstly, it is very overwhelming with its number of rooms, hotspots, and items. It is not rare to be in a situation where you have more than 20 items in your inventory and can theoretically combine them with probably more than 200 things spread across... like 20–30 rooms? This gets incredibly annoying if you happen to get stuck because if you want to brute-force this, you're up for at least 1-2 hours of trying everything on everything, and you might still miss that one interaction that you're supposed to do. It sadly doesn't help that there are so many voiced lines because at times it's difficult to assess what is helpful info and what is just random blabbering. Especially since the game is set in an asylum.

The second thing is connected to the first and it's the moon logic of the puzzles. I consider myself fairly good at puzzles and have finished the last 5 or so adventure games without ever looking anything up. I don't know if I'm operating on a completely different wavelength than Poki (the designer), but I just don't understand his puzzles and find them pretty annoying most of the time. In my 4 hours or so of gameplay, I was already forced about 4 times to consult a walkthrough, and every single time my reaction wasn't "that was so obvious" but "how the hell was I ever supposed to figure that out". One example in recent memory, very mild puzzle spoiler: [spoiler] In order to get to a laundry room, you need a blanket on the floor (don't even ask). To get the blanket, you need to use scissors on a person who wears a sweater and sits on the blanket, then you need to repeat the steps to get in their room (you can't just leave the room and get back, nothing happens), and after you're there, you can't just take the blanket; you need to put a cookie on it so it gets dirty. Then you need to leave the room again, and it will appear in the laundry room the next time you get there. [/spoiler] The whole game is like this.

Another bad thing is the controls. I don't understand why anyone would use anything else than simple look/interact unless it's innovative or somehow beneficial to the gameplay. Edna & Harvey uses this annoying wheel that you need to use every time unless you want to use the "default action," which you have no idea what actually is. There are both pick-up and interact actions, and you never quite know which one to use, and it's always the second one you try. I've heard some obnoxious variant of "this is too big to carry around" about a million times, but you still can't count on it because there's a lot of pretty big items that you CAN carry around. It's just so annoying that you can't just have right-click to look at and left-click to interact with like 90% of well-designed adventure games.

I appreciate the mood of the game, and I recognize that there's a certain quality under all these issues (and I didn't even mention bugs...), but I simply can't recommend it. And frankly, I'm a little shocked it has 92% positive reviews on Steam.

I found the voice acting on Edna, Harvey and Babbitt to be a little grating and the dialogue not the best.

The puzzles were also unintuitive, especially getting past the guard at the beginning.

It did get better later in the game as more characters got introduced, but it was too little, too late and I had already mostly lost interest in the plot or puzzles by that point.

While I will admit this game is charming with its world, characters and art-style, it has some majors downsides that would probably turn you off if you aren't used to these kind of games(I'm sure as hell am not). First for what I like: The art-work is charming and nice to look at despite how amateurish it looks although I'm certain that is done on purpose. I also really like the overall story and setup which lends itself well to a point and click adventure. Having to escape an asylum isn't the most unique concept on its own, but having it relate to this sort of puzzle solving game-play really adds to it. Now for the games issues, first of which the puzzles. A majority of the time the solutions to puzzles aren't don't make much sense or aren't even alluded to. Take for example the Limo Driver; if you go upstairs and then to find your way down He will be there blocking your entry, but you can't use the laundry lift because its shutdown. My idea was that maybe I have to activate the lift; maybe use an electrical box to turn it on. I tried turning off all the lights to see if it would do anything, but nothing worked, until I went online and saw that in order to get back down you had to go to the break-room, open the window and use the gumball machine. The game never alluded to it and you would've never assumed that was the solution. The solutions to puzzles often aren't even related to the issue or are never even hinted at. Overall while this game was charming and has a fun story with kooky characters the vagueness of puzzles leaves me thinking it could've been better.

The remastered visuals look nice; I only wish they would speed up animations (or let the player skip them) and make location transitions easier to spot without using the highlight tool, but alas. However, the interface remains cumbersome, the puzzles require much guesswork, and the game may take a little too long to get into due to the amount of inane dialogue - in the beginning especially. While that is very much in line with the setting of the game - the mental hospital - it does not make the interactions easier to follow (though this does make the game more challenging).

On the other hand, the game deserves praise for including so many lines of unique dialogue for interactions - if you enjoy listening to the characters speak, you can cycle through all available actions as well as all the inventory items on every interactive spot (a few achievements are built around this). Harvey, for one, almost always has something outlandish to say.

The game took around 12 hours.

The puzzle in the beginning is broken, [spoiler] the guard is simultaneously in the room and in front of the cell [/spoiler] and the most other puzzles are either made artificially long by have too many steps or the puzzles are far fetched.

And as for the ending: it isn't worth all the hassle you need to go through.

There is a bug near the middle of the game which makes it impossible to complete the game. Didn't find a patch or savegame to fix it.

Refund request denied, because I played for more than 2 hours. Waste of 20 bucks.

I've come from a background of the Deponia series, The Inner World, Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes, Broken Age, Machinarium, and possibly a few more.

This game has been a wild ride, though this has probably been the most boring adventure game I've played, and I've played a whole lot of adventure games.

The psych ward setting just doesn't feel very fun compared to the awe-inspiring settings I've seen inside of other adventure games. The main character Edna isn't exactly relatable either, and is actually super annoying to listen to at times.

I can tell the developers put a lot of love into this game as there's so many small, unexpected things you can do, though sometimes I wonder if all that extra effort was worth it.

Please take this review with a grain of salt as I haven't actually completed the game, though it's hard to find the motivation to actually finish this.
